title: Eliphaz Accuses Job and Calls Him to Return
summary: Eliphaz opens the third cycle by arguing that God gains nothing from human righteousness, so Job's suffering must be punishment for great sin. He then invents a list of crimes: exploiting debtors, refusing water and bread to the needy, turning widows away, crushing orphans. He ends with a warm call to reconcile with God, promising that if Job returns, the Almighty will be his treasure, his prayers will be heard, and he will even intercede for others.
story: The third and final cycle of speeches begins here (chapters 22 to 27). In chapter 21 Job argued that the wicked often prosper, which undercut the friends' whole system. Eliphaz, the eldest and most measured of the three, cannot allow that. In chapters 4 and 5 he spoke gently and assumed Job was basically righteous. In chapter 15 he accused Job of undermining piety with his words. Now, with no evidence at all, he charges Job with specific crimes. The logic is simple: God punishes sin, Job is suffering greatly, therefore Job's sin must be great. Job will answer these charges directly in his great oath of innocence in chapter 31. The chapter's final promise contains an irony the reader will only see at the end: in 42:8 it is Job who prays for Eliphaz.
historical:
The setting is the same undated patriarchal world of Uz, where Job has been described as the greatest man among all the people of the East (1:3). Eliphaz's accusations assume the social position such a man held. A great landowner was expected to act as protector of the vulnerable in his region, lending to those in need, providing for widows and orphans, and judging disputes fairly. Rulers across the ancient Near East boasted of doing exactly this; the prologue and epilogue of Hammurabi's law code (from Babylon, around the eighteenth century BC) claim that the king was appointed so that the strong would not oppress the weak and so that justice would be done for the orphan and the widow.

Verse 24 mentions the gold of Ophir, famous in the Old Testament as a source of the finest gold, which Solomon's fleets are said to have brought back (1 Kings 9:28). Its location is unknown. Proposals include southern Arabia, the coast of East Africa, and India. An ostracon (an inscribed pottery shard) found at Tell Qasile, near modern Tel Aviv, mentions gold of Ophir, which shows the phrase was a recognized trade term.
cultural:
Eliphaz's list draws on customs that Israel's law also addresses. Taking a pledge (verse 6) meant holding some item of a borrower's property as security for a loan. For the poor, often the only thing of value was a cloak, which also served as a blanket at night. Israel's law required a creditor to return such a cloak before sunset (Exodus 22:26-27). To strip the naked of their clothing is to take even that. Refusing water and bread to travelers or the hungry (verse 7) violated the ancient duty of hospitality, and sending widows away empty-handed (verse 9) was a well-known mark of injustice, since widows and orphans had no male protector to speak for them in court.

Eliphaz also puts words in Job's mouth (verses 13-14): What does God know? Does he judge through thick darkness? Ancient people often pictured the sky as a vault or circle over the earth, with God enthroned above it and hidden by clouds. Eliphaz accuses Job of thinking that these clouds keep God from seeing. Job has never said this. In fact his complaint has been that God sees him too closely (7:17-20).
literary: The speech has three movements. First comes an argument (verses 2-5): a series of rhetorical questions insisting that God has nothing to gain from Job and therefore cannot be punishing him for his piety, so it must be for his wickedness. Second comes the indictment (verses 6-20), a list of specific charges followed by the consequences (snares, darkness, flood) and a warning that Job is walking the ancient path of wicked men, whose foundations were swept away by a flood, which many interpreters take as an allusion to the generation of Noah's flood. Verse 18 repeats almost word for word a line Job had just spoken (21:16), as if Eliphaz is throwing Job's words back at him. The third movement (verses 21-30) is a call to repentance and a series of promises, the most beautiful poetry in any of the friends' speeches. The contrast between the harsh middle and the tender end is striking, and it shows Eliphaz as a man who sincerely believes that accusing Job is the first step in helping him.

outline.t: God gains nothing from you; your sin must be great
Eliphaz's list of Job's supposed crimes
You think God cannot see; remember the fate of the wicked
Return to the Almighty and be restored

doctrines.note: Eliphaz's call to return to the Almighty (verse 23) is good counsel in itself, and his promise that God will become Job's treasure (verse 25) is a genuine insight into what repentance brings. His mistake is urging repentance for sins Job did not commit.

Eliphaz says God gains nothing from human righteousness (verses 2-3). There is truth here: God does not need anything from his creatures. But Eliphaz draws the wrong conclusion, that God is indifferent to the righteous. The book's prologue shows the opposite: God delights in Job (1:8).

The promise that God will hear the returning sinner's prayer and deliver others through him (verses 27-30) comes true at the end of the book in a way Eliphaz never expected, when Job prays for his friends and God accepts his prayer (42:8-10).

words.note: Sakan, to be of use or benefit. It appears three times in this chapter and opens Eliphaz's argument: Can a man be of use to God? The question assumes that God relates to people only in terms of profit or loss. The prologue, in which the Accuser asks whether Job fears God for nothing (1:9), has already raised the question of motive in the opposite direction.

Chaval, to take a pledge. It describes seizing a borrower's property as security for a debt. Eliphaz's first accusation (verse 6) is that Job took pledges needlessly, exploiting his own relatives. The same practice is regulated in Israel's law to protect the poor.

Shuv, to return or turn back. It is the Old Testament's central word for repentance, a turning back to God. Eliphaz uses it in verse 23. The prophets use the same verb again and again in their calls to Israel.

Betser, gold ore or precious metal. It appears twice, in verses 24 and 25. Eliphaz tells Job to throw his gold into the dust, and then the Almighty will be his gold. The wordplay makes the point: God himself is the treasure that replaces all others.

christ: Eliphaz speaks better than he knows in his closing promise. He says that the one who returns to God will intercede for others, and that even the guilty will be delivered through the cleanness of that person's hands (verse 30). At the end of the book God tells Eliphaz that Job, the man he wrongly accused, must pray for him, and that God will accept Job's prayer (42:8). The pattern of a righteous one interceding for the guilty is fulfilled supremely in Jesus, who prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34) and who, according to Hebrews 7:25, always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through him. The connection is typological, a pattern rather than a prediction. Eliphaz's theology would have treated Jesus on the cross as a man suffering for his own sins; the gospel reveals a righteous man suffering for the sins of others and praying for them as he did.

hard.q: Why does Eliphaz accuse Job of crimes he never committed?
hard.a: Nothing in the book supports Eliphaz's charges. The narrator and God both call Job blameless and upright (1:1, 1:8, 2:3), and Job's own later description of his life (chapters 29 and 31) presents him as a defender of widows, orphans, and the poor. The most common explanation is that Eliphaz reasons backward from his theology. If God always punishes in proportion to sin, then great suffering proves great sin, and Eliphaz simply supplies the sins his system requires. Some interpreters add that he picks the most likely crimes for a wealthy man, the kind of abuse the powerful were known for. Others note that Eliphaz may sincerely believe he is doing Job a kindness, since naming the sin is the first step toward the restoration he promises at the end. On every reading, the chapter is a sober warning about what happens when a theological system is trusted more than a person's testimony and God's own verdict.

questions: Eliphaz invents Job's sins to fit his theology. Have you ever assumed someone must have done something wrong because of what happened to them?
Eliphaz says the Almighty will be Job's gold (verse 25). What would it mean for God himself, not his gifts, to be your treasure?
At the end of the book, the man Eliphaz accused prays for him. What does that reversal suggest about how God deals with those who have wronged us?
